niche: a UK mutual home insurer's board choosing which of four regional home books takes a 2027 catastrophe excess of loss layer (GBP 15 million excess of 10 million each loss occurrence, one reinstatement), valued as the expected 2027 recoveries on its own 2010 to 2025 storm, flood and freeze events brought to the 2027 book less the premium and the expected reinstatement premium, when what a claim costs rises with the claims each repair panel firm has to take on at once and one region's book doubled in 2021 while its panel did not grow
answer: Pennine: the layer is worth GBP 0.1 million a year in 2027, against Severn Vale at GBP 0.0 million, Coastal North at -0.5 and Fenland at -0.8
analyst_test: A strong analyst who reads every file correctly builds each year's loss occurrences under the hours clause, brings every claim to 2027 by its district's policies against the year's and by the rebuild cost index against its month of loss, and names Severn Vale at GBP 0.0 million (Pennine -0.4); reading RC-07 s.3 (the index is a standard rebuild's price in ordinary times) and adding the surge the field reads on a catastrophe's size, by its claim count or its loss in any of 16 forms, still names Severn Vale, because no field or document says that what a claim costs depends on how many claims the region's panel firms have to repair at once; the golden prices each event at the repair cost its 2027 claims per panel firm imply and names Pennine at GBP 0.1 million.
domain_test: The deciding quantity is a catastrophe layer's expected recoveries, which a reinsurance actuary prices from the company's event losses brought to the cover year's exposure and costs; catastrophe modelling knows that claim costs rise with an event's size when local repair capacity is overwhelmed (post-event demand surge), so an event striking a larger book costs more than proportionally more where the repair capacity has not grown.
layer1: event codes only for declared events; storm claims coded at first notice, freeze claims often notified weeks late and without the code; occurrences built from dates of loss under the hours clause, one period from each catastrophe's first loss
incurred as paid plus outstanding on 31 October 2026, a few 2025 claims still reserved
cash settlements carry no panel firm or sign-off date; repairs signed off months after the loss
the 1 January 2021 Calder and Colne book transfer into eight Pennine districts, policies by district and year
ordinary windstorm, flood and freeze claims on quiet days and inside the catastrophe periods
stakeholder_role: the head of reinsurance preparing the board's placement paper
driver: An event's loss carried to a larger book is scaled claim by claim at the cost each claim carried, when what a claim costs rises with how many claims the region's repair capacity has to take on at once; where the book has grown and the capacity has not, the same event costs more per claim at the forward scale, and only the cost per claim read against claims per unit of capacity across every event shows by how much.
driver_concrete: Each 2010 to 2025 storm, flood and freeze is re-costed as it would strike the 2027 book: its claims scaled by district policies, each claim's cost re-read from the cost per claim against claims per panel firm at the event's 2027 claims per firm (Pennine's panel stayed at 30 to 34 firms while its book doubled with the 2021 transfer), and the layer applied to the occurrences the hours clause allows.
stump: A competent analyst brings every claim to 2027 by its district's policies and the rebuild cost index, adds at most the surge the field reads on a catastrophe's size, applies the layer to the occurrences the hours clause allows and names Severn Vale (GBP 0.0 million at the index alone), where the golden is Pennine at GBP 0.1 million; the step that lands it there is pricing a historical event's claims at the cost each claim carried at the event's own load on the repair panel, when Pennine's four pre-2021 freezes, struck at 22.6 to 25.1 claims a panel firm, would put 44 to 50 claims on each of its 34 firms in 2027.

lineage.niche: which of a bike-share operator's five classic networks gets 300 e-bikes and the net fare revenue a year they add, when the busiest network's stations rarely run dry and the campus network's residence-hall hubs run dry at every teaching-weekday class change, so the rides on record understate the requests
lineage.driver: A launch's added revenue is sized from requests, but the record holds only the requests the service met: where the existing supply runs out at every peak, the unmet requests leave no row, so carrying a pilot's uplift by each candidate's recorded use sends the launch to the candidate whose supply never runs out; only the supply rebuilt second by second from the movements in and out shows which candidate turns away the most requests.
lineage.driver_concrete: Each network's turned-away requests are rebuilt from each station's classic stock (the 03:00 audit, then every undock, dock and van move, second by second) and its requests per stocked second by month, day type and hour, and University, whose residence-hall hubs run dry at every class change, adds the most net fare revenue, while Central, with the most rides on record, rarely runs dry.
lineage.stump: A competent analyst carries the pilot's e-bike share and new-rider uplift to each network's 2025 rides and names Central at about USD 50,000 a year, against University at USD 125,000, whose residence-hall hubs turn away the class-change requests the trip record never shows.
lineage.fate: spent at stage 4 (2026-10-26): both scored readers landed the call (University) by rebuilding the empty-dock seconds; the judge returned SEND_BACK on the grain and the induced riders
